text: BCP Table 2902.1 establishes minimum plumbing fixture counts by occupancy. For an apartment house, the table includes one water closet, one lavatory and one bathtub/shower per dwelling unit, plus a kitchen sink per dwelling unit and an automatic clothes-washer connection per 20 dwelling units. Fixture counts are not the same as pump design flow; pump flow must be determined using the applicable hydraulic demand method. text: ASHRAE 2023 Handbook—HVAC Applications, Chapter 51 states that hot-water recirculation loops are commonly used where piping is long and hot water is desired quickly at fixtures. Return piping and a circulation device are provided; most systems use circulating pumps. Pump controls may use a return-line thermostat, time switch, or demand/on-demand methods such as manual initiation, flow switches or occupancy sensors. Controls that operate only when needed can reduce heat loss and pumping energy. text: ASHRAE 2023 Chapter 51 states that for larger hot-water recirculation installations, piping heat losses should be determined from the total length of hot-water supply and return piping and an appropriate heat-loss factor from engineering data or insulation/manufacturer data. The required circulation pump flow is then determined from the total heat loss and the allowable temperature drop: Qp = q/(rho cp Δt). For water, the chapter gives rho about 0.99 kg/L at 50°C and cp = 4186.8 J/(kg·K). The allowable temperature drop is a design input; the example cautions that assuming a 10 K drop means accepting that drop at the last fixture. The pump is then selected to provide the required flow and the pressure/head at that flow is obtained from the pump curve. text: ASHRAE 2023 Chapter 51 separates recirculation flow sizing from pump pressure selection: after calculating the circulation flow from heat loss and allowable temperature drop, select a pump for that flow and obtain the pressure created at that flow from the pump curve. PumpDesign AI should therefore calculate the loop hydraulic resistance from the actual return/supply circuit and report the pump duty point as required flow at required loop head; it should not infer pump head from heat loss alone. text: ASHRAE 2023 Chapter 51 states that hot-water supply piping is hydraulically sized using the same pressure-drop principles as cold-water piping, while the piping system should meet peak demand at acceptable pressure loss. It also cautions against oversizing hot-water pipes because larger diameter can increase heat loss, delivery delay and lower flow velocity. For recirculation systems, return piping must be sized for the required circulation flow and acceptable pressure loss using the actual loop layout and selected design method. metadata.text: ASHRAE 2023 Chapter 51 states that hot-water supply piping is hydraulically sized using the same pressure-drop principles as cold-water piping, while the piping system should meet peak demand at acceptable pressure loss. It also cautions against oversizing hot-water pipes because larger diameter can increase heat loss, delivery delay and lower flow velocity. For recirculation systems, return piping must be sized for the required circulation flow and acceptable pressure loss using the actual loop layout and selected design method.

PumpDesign AI should therefore report the heat-loss basis and control strategy alongside the hydraulic pump duty. text: PumpDesign AI must not use one universal Hazen-Williams C value. ASHRAE Chapter 22 states typical C=150 for plastic pipe and copper tubing, C=140 for new steel pipe, and values down to 100 and below for badly corroded or very rough pipe. A broader secondary engineering table provides condition-dependent values/ranges for ABS, aluminum, asbestos cement, brass, cast iron by age/lining, concrete, copper, ductile iron, FRP, galvanized iron, PE, PVC, steel, vitrified clay, wrought iron and wood. DIPRA specifically recommends C=140 for cement-mortar-lined cast and ductile iron based on field testing. The software must preserve source/range/status and allow an engineer override.
